factProposals.value: Workers are real, separate OS processes forked by ProcessWorkerPool (workerProcess.ts), each running a standing consumer loop on the Redis Streams consumer group. The autoscaler sizes the pool from the group's lag.
Autoscaling is single-host: the pool forks child processes on the machine running the autoscaler. Scaling across machines or containers is not built.
Queue depth comes from Redis 7+ XINFO GROUPS lag (undelivered entries), not XLEN. When Redis can't compute lag the read throws BacklogUnknownError rather than returning 0.

decisions.statement: Scale up immediately; scale down only after the backlog has stayed below the current worker count's need for scaleDownAfter consecutive evaluations.
decisions.rationale: a growing backlog is the expensive case, while killing workers during a brief lull between bursts just forces a respawn moments later (flapping).

decisions.statement: The pool never respawns a dead worker itself; the autoscaler's next evaluation sees the lower count and scales back up.
decisions.rationale: keeps exactly one place deciding how many workers exist, so the logged scaling decisions are the complete story of the pool's size.

decisions.statement: Each evaluation mints its own correlation ID and passes it to every worker it spawns, which logs worker_started and worker_stopped with it.
decisions.rationale: makes 'why does this worker exist' answerable from logs alone, tracing any worker back to the scaling decision that created it.

decisions.statement: An unreadable or hung backlog read holds the current worker count instead of assuming 0.
decisions.rationale: assuming 0 would scale down a backlog the system simply can't see, the worst possible response to a Redis blip.

limitations.statement: Each worker process has its own in-memory idempotency store. Correct today because a consumer group delivers each entry to one consumer, but a redelivered entry landing on a different worker would not be caught as a duplicate.
dequeueOne() acks on delivery, so a worker killed mid-job loses that job rather than leaving it claimable. Ack-after-processing and redelivery belong to STORY-008's retry policy.
Worker count and autoscale events are not yet shown on the SLO dashboard (STORY-005); they are visible in structured logs and Autoscaler.status() only.
